ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Otolaryngology (head and neck surgery) Consultation — Jim Thorpe — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Lip biopsy result and otolaryngology (head and neck surgery) consultation; echocardiogram and readiness for surgery

text.paragraph: Suspected squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lip in a 63-year-old former athlete with decades of outdoor work and about 35 pack-years of smoking, who also has chronic coronary disease with stable angina eight years after a heart attack. An incisional biopsy was taken on the day of this referral. Please confirm the diagnosis and stage, advise on treatment and the neck, advise on surgery with his heart disease and new aspirin, and set the surveillance plan. [S]
Urgency: Within one to two weeks, when the biopsy result is available. [S]

list.item: Does the biopsy confirm squamous cell carcinoma, and what is the clinical stage?
What treatment do you advise for the primary, with what margins, and how will his lip look and work afterwards?
Does he need imaging or treatment of the neck?
Can surgery proceed safely with his coronary disease, and should aspirin and metoprolol be continued?
What surveillance and prevention do you advise afterwards?

text.paragraph: Mr. Thorpe, a 63-year-old coach and speaker, is seen at the request of Dr. Fairbanks one week after an incisional biopsy of a lower lip sore present for about three months. He has worked outdoors for most of his life and smoked until eight years ago. He has no lip numbness, mouth pain, trouble swallowing, or neck lumps. He has stable exertional angina and started aspirin, atorvastatin and metoprolol a week ago. He wants to know how the operation will affect the look and use of his lip and whether he can keep coaching. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: James Francis Thorpe was born a twin on the Sac and Fox reservation near present Prague, Oklahoma, to Hiram and Charlotte Vieux Thorpe. His Sac and Fox name, Wa-tho-huck, means "Bright Path." He is usually considered Sac and Fox and was brought up as a member of the Sac and Fox tribe; he also had Potawatomi, Kickapoo, Menominee, Irish and French ancestry. The Oklahoma Historical Society gives his birth as May 28, 1888, noting that his estate cites 1887; another reference work gives May 22, 1887. [D]
His twin brother, Charles, died of pneumonia just short of their eighth birthday; his mother died when he was twelve and his father when he was sixteen. [D]

He attended federal boarding schools, including the Sac and Fox Indian Agency School, Haskell Institute, and from 1903 the Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania, where he became a track and football star. [D]

At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm he won gold medals in the pentathlon and decathlon. In January 1913 the Amateur Athletic Union stripped him of his medals because he had played semiprofessional baseball; in 1982 the International Olympic Committee recognized him as co-winner, and on July 15, 2022 it restored him as sole winner of both events. [D]

He played major-league baseball from 1913 to 1919 and professional football into 1928, and was the first president of the American Professional Football Association, the forerunner of the National Football League. Afterwards he worked as a film extra and in construction, as a security guard and ditch digger, at the Ford plant in Dearborn during the Second World War, and in the Merchant Marine in 1945; he became a critic of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, lectured widely, and worked to inspire American Indians. [D]

He reportedly had an alcohol problem; one reference work states that excessive drinking began at Carlisle and troubled him for the rest of his life and frustrated his attempts at a stable married life. [D]
In 1951 he was treated for lip cancer as a charity patient in a Philadelphia hospital, where he had an operation. [D]
He had a heart attack in 1943. [D]
In 1950 an Associated Press poll named him the greatest athlete of the first half of the twentieth century. [D]

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lip (C00.1). Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip, 1.2 cm, with no palpable nodes: clinical T1 N0 (AJCC 8th edition, lip and oral cavity). Surgery is the preferred treatment. A V-excision with 5 to 10 mm clinical margins and frozen-section control of the margins, closed directly, removes up to a third of the lower lip with good function and appearance. Lower lip cancers of this size rarely spread to the neck; a contrast CT of the neck is reasonable before surgery to stage it, and elective neck dissection is not needed if the final depth of invasion is small, generally under 4 mm, with clear margins. Radiation is an alternative but is not preferred for a small, resectable lesion. [S]

Chronic coronary disease with stable angina (I25.119). An excision under local anesthesia is a low-risk operation. With stable angina, an ejection fraction of 55%, and no heart failure, no further cardiac testing is needed. Aspirin should be continued because bleeding from a lip excision is easily controlled, and metoprolol should not be stopped. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Biopsy: invasive, well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Dr. Fairbanks's intake note. Echocardiogram this morning: left ventricular ejection fraction 55%, old inferior wall motion abnormality, no significant valve disease. Resting ECG: sinus rhythm with old inferior Q waves. Hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, platelets 231 x10^3/uL, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL. [S]

list.item: Contrast CT of the neck before surgery. [S]
V-excision of the lower lip cancer under local anesthesia with 5 to 10 mm margins and frozen-section margin control, with primary closure, in about two weeks. [S]
No elective neck dissection if the final depth of invasion is small and the margins are clear; re-excision if a margin is involved. [S]
Continue aspirin 81 mg and metoprolol through surgery; acetaminophen for pain afterwards. [S]

Surveillance by history and examination of the lips, mouth and neck every 1 to 3 months in the first year, every 2 to 6 months in the second, every 4 to 8 months in years 3 to 5, then yearly; imaging only for symptoms or findings. [S]
Daily lip balm with sunscreen and a hat, yearly skin examination, staying tobacco-free, and a dental check-up. [S]
Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT if he is eligible, because of his smoking history. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Fairbanks, who sees him the same day. Mr. Thorpe asked many questions; the operation, the expected scar and lip function, and his return to coaching within about a week were explained, and he agreed to the plan. He decides who else receives this note. [S]

Follow-up: Surgery in about two weeks; post-operative check by the surgical team at one week for suture removal; pathology reviewed with Dr. Fairbanks at two weeks; surveillance shared with Dr. Fairbanks. [S]
